title: Verbs that never change
goal: Meet the heart of the language: one verb form for every person and every time, and four small words that place the action in the past, the present or the future without touching the verb at all.
bekal: use *makan*, *minum*, *pergi*, *pulang* and twenty other verbs in any sentence
say what you have done, are doing, have not yet done and will do
answer the question that every Indonesian will ask you: *Sudah makan?*

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Jam satu siang di kantor
dialogs.intro: One o'clock in the afternoon. Rina finds Sarah still at her desk.

lines.speaker: Rina:
lines.id: Come on, let's eat! I haven't either.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Sebentar, ya. Saya sedang kirim email.
lines.id: Just a moment. I'm sending an email.
lines.literal: a-moment, yes. I in-the-middle-of send email.

lines.speaker: Rina:
lines.text: Oke. Nanti kita pergi ke warung depan.
lines.id: OK. Later we'll go to the food stall out front.
lines.literal: OK. later we go to stall front.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.id: What time does that stall open?

lines.speaker: Rina:
lines.text: Sudah buka dari pagi. Tutup jam sembilan malam.
lines.id: It's been open since morning. It closes at nine at night.
lines.literal: already open from morning. close hour nine night.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Bagus. Saya akan pesan nasi goreng.
lines.literal: good. I will order rice fried.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.id: I do, but not too spicy.

lines.speaker: Rina:
lines.id: That's fine. Come on, are you done?

notes: **Sudah makan? is a greeting as much as a question.** Asking whether someone has eaten is a standard piece of Indonesian friendliness, roughly where the British would say "you all right?". You may answer honestly, but nobody is planning your lunch.

**Belum, not tidak.** Sarah has not eaten *yet*, and Indonesian has a dedicated word for that. Answering *tidak* would mean "no, I don't eat" — a statement about your habits, not about today. This distinction is genuinely important and Unit 6 nails it down.
**Sudah and belum are complete answers.** "Have you eaten?" — *Sudah.* "Are you married?" — *Belum.* One word, no verb repeated. It is the same instinct you saw with *ada* in Unit 2.

**Ayo!** is the invitation particle: "come on, let's". *Ayo makan!* (let's eat), *Ayo pergi!* (let's go), *Ayo!* on its own (come on!). Its cousin *mari* is the formal version, which you will hear in announcements and speeches.

**Nasi goreng, not goreng nasi.** *Goreng* means "fried", and the adjective follows the noun, exactly as *buku ini* and *buku saya* did. Every Indonesian dish name you already know obeys this: *nasi goreng*, *mie goreng*, *ayam bakar*, *es teh manis*.

grammars.title: The verb does not move
body: Write out any English verb in all its forms and count them: eat, eats, ate, eaten, eating. Now Indonesian:

head: Indonesian
English
rows: I eat. / I am eating. / I ate.

after: One form, *makan*, in every line. What changes is a time word elsewhere in the sentence — *kemarin*, *besok* — or nothing at all, because the situation already makes it clear.

This is why Indonesian is the fastest major language to start speaking. Every verb you learn is learned once, completely, forever. There is no conjugation table anywhere in this book, and there is none in the language.

grammars.title: The four time markers
body: These are Indonesian's answer to tense. Each one sits **before** the verb.
after: 💬 *Sedang* is the written form; in conversation almost everyone says *lagi*. *Lagi apa?* — "what are you doing?" — is one of the most common text messages in the country.

**Akan is often left out.** If the sentence already contains *besok* or *nanti*, the future is obvious and Indonesians drop *akan* entirely: *Besok saya ke Bandung* — "tomorrow I go to Bandung". Adding it is never wrong, just a little formal.

⚠️ Do not stack *sudah* with a past-time word thinking it makes the sentence more past. *Kemarin saya sudah makan* is fine but means "yesterday I had already eaten" — the *sudah* still means "already".

sections.title: Twenty verbs to own this week

blocks.text: These are root forms — the shape you say, and the shape you look up. None of them will ever change.

Two verbs behave slightly unusually and are worth a note. *Pulang* means specifically "to go home" — one word for the whole idea, and Indonesians use it constantly. *Mandi* means to bathe, and in Indonesia that usually means twice a day; *Sudah mandi?* is a perfectly normal question between family or friends.
Indonesian puts verbs straight after one another with nothing in between — no "to", no changes.

head: Indonesian
Word for word
English
rows: I want to try eating it.
I was about to go home.

blocks.text: The markers stack in the same easy way, and their order matches the order of the English words: *sudah mau* ("already about to"), *belum bisa* ("can't yet"), *masih mau* ("still want"), *tidak akan* ("will not").

Two more time words to add now, because you will need them in every sentence: *nanti* (later today) and *tadi* (earlier today). *Tadi saya makan* — "I ate earlier". *Nanti saya telepon* — "I'll call you later".

items: We want to eat fried rice.
